planting.note: Plant tubers once soil has warmed; grows best beside a shaded water feature or boggy bed.

directions: This Yunnan and northern Indochina stream-bank aroid forms a clump of glossy, Colocasia-like leaves from a short rhizome and wants the same damp, shaded niche it occupies on forest floors. Keep the root zone constantly moist to boggy rather than merely watered, and give it dappled or full shade since the foliage scorches in direct sun. Where winters drop below the mid-20s°F, lift the rhizome or grow it in a container that can be moved under cover, since it has no meaningful frost tolerance. A small, greenish-yellow aroid spadix appears among the leaves but the plant is grown primarily for its bold tropical foliage effect at pond edges and shade borders.

planting.note: Set tubers out after the last hard frost into humus-rich woodland soil.

directions: Native to woodland floors across central and southern China, this tuberous aroid sends up a dark purple-tinged spathe on a short stalk before its arrow-shaped leaves unfurl each spring. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained shade soil that stays evenly moist through the growing season, then let it dry down somewhat as the foliage yellows and the tuber enters summer or autumn dormancy. It tolerates brief cold spells better than many tropical aroids but still benefits from a thick mulch layer in the coldest part of its range. In China the tuber is the source of the traditional medicinal material known as bai fu zi, though garden plants are grown strictly as woodland curiosities.

planting.note: Plant small tubers in warm shaded soil once nights stay above 55°F.

directions: Found on shaded slopes and forest margins from Taiwan through southern China and into Southeast Asia, this diminutive tuberous aroid is grown by collectors for its paired, flag-like green-and-maroon spathes held just above a low rosette of arrow-shaped leaves. It thrives in loose, humus-rich soil under high shade with regular moisture during active growth, then wants to stay drier once the foliage dies back for its dry-season dormancy. Because the tuber is small and shallow, a container or raised woodland bed makes winter protection and lifting far easier than in open ground. Treat it as a tender novelty groundcover for a shaded patio collection rather than a hardy landscape perennial.

planting.note: Plant tubers in warm, shaded humus-rich soil after danger of frost.

directions: Widespread across the forest floors of India and Southeast Asia, this small tuberous aroid produces a short, purplish-brown spathe close to the ground followed by a scattering of arrow-shaped leaves on thin petioles. Give it dappled to deep shade and loose, moisture-retentive soil during the monsoon-like growing flush, then allow the soil to dry as the plant collapses into its tuber for a dry-season rest. It has no cold tolerance to speak of, so gardeners outside the tropics grow it as a container specimen that can be moved indoors or stored dry over winter. In the garden it works best tucked among larger shade aroids where its subtle, ground-hugging habit can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant tubers once soil is workable in spring, well before the single leaf emerges.

directions: Native to shaded hillside woodland on Kyushu in southern Japan, this is one of the cold-hardiest members of its genus and can overwinter outdoors in milder temperate gardens with a protective mulch. A single deeply divided leaf rises each year from an underground tuber, followed in some seasons by a modest mottled spathe with the characteristic faint carrion scent of the genus. Plant it in rich, well-drained woodland soil in dappled shade and keep it evenly moist through the growing season, then withhold water once the leaf yellows and the tuber goes dormant for winter. It is sold by specialty perennial nurseries as a curiosity for shade gardeners wanting a hardier alternative to tropical Amorphophallus species.

planting.note: Plant tubers in loose, humus-rich shaded soil after the last frost.

directions: This smaller-growing Amorphophallus comes from shaded limestone woodland in Yunnan province, China, where it emerges from a flattened tuber with a single divided leaf each growing season. It prefers loose, fast-draining but humus-rich soil in dappled to deep shade, with consistent moisture while the leaf is active and a dry rest once it dies back for dormancy. Occasional specimens produce a compact, mottled spathe typical of the genus, but the plant is mainly grown by aroid collectors for its manageable size compared to giant relatives. Because it has essentially no frost tolerance, gardeners outside its native range grow it in pots that can be sheltered or stored dry through winter.
